story.headline: Democrats take both houses of Congress
story.summary: Democrats won majorities in both the US House and Senate in the 3 November 2026 midterms, flipping Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Maine and Michigan.
story.display_body: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the US midterm elections on Tuesday 3 November, the first time since 2006 that a sitting Republican president has lost both chambers. By the Associated Press tally relayed by Al Jazeera on Wednesday morning, Democrats had won 228 House seats and led in 34 more (218 is a majority), and had won 54 Senate seats (51 is a majority); counting continues and several races are uncalled. They flipped Senate seats in states Republicans have long held: James Talarico beat Ken Paxton in Texas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas since 1932, Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins in Maine, and Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate. Speaking to Fox News, Donald Trump congratulated the Democrats and said he would accept the results, but added "I wasn't on the ballot", and he posted an image of a red cap reading "Veto" on Truth Social.
story.why: from January, legislation, budgets and investigations will need a Democratic Congress, so Trump will have to rely on his veto and on executive action for the second half of his term, including over the Iran war.

story.headline: Trump says Israel military aid will end
story.summary: Trump said on Fox News the US will end its roughly $3.8bn annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, two years before the memorandum expires.
story.display_body: On Tuesday 3 November, Donald Trump said in a Fox News interview that the US will stop paying Israel's roughly $3.8 billion a year in military aid by the end of 2026, and that Israel is "fine" with this. The aid comes under a 10-year memorandum of understanding that began in 2019 and runs until September 2028. Trump said he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had "made a deal months ago", but he did not explain how the agreement would end early, and no written US or Israeli statement has been published. He said Israel could still buy US weapons "whenever they want". Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to form a coalition to replace Netanyahu, said Israel's defence establishment had learned of the change "through the media".
story.why: this would be the biggest change in US military support for Israel in decades, but for now it rests only on a TV interview.

story.headline: Israel certifies election, rejects fraud claims
story.summary: Israel's Central Elections Committee certified the 27 October Knesset election results on 4 November after finding no fraud.
story.display_body: On Wednesday 4 November, Israel's Central Elections Committee certified the results of the Knesset election of 27 October, saying a review of 9,069 polling stations found no irregularities that changed the outcome. Committee chair Noam Sohlberg, a Supreme Court justice, handed the results to President Isaac Herzog and said those casting doubt on them pose "a real danger" to Israel's democracy. Likud and Shas abstained in the committee's vote, and Sohlberg cast the deciding vote. Netanyahu and his allies have claimed, without evidence, that Arab-led parties "stole" the election; National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir repeated that claim and said his Otzma Yehudit party would vote against approving the results. Herzog is meeting the parties, which have not yet formed a majority.
story.why: the certification removes the formal basis for Likud's challenge and moves the fight to coalition talks, where Netanyahu's opponents are lining up behind Eisenkot.

story.headline: Greenland parliament approves US defence deal
story.summary: Greenland's parliament adopted the trilateral defence agreement with Denmark and the US allowing two new US bases; Denmark votes on 19 November.
story.display_body: On Tuesday 3 November, Greenland's parliament, Inatsisartut, adopted the defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States, which allows two new US military bases on the island. The agreement, signed in September in New York by Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, amends the 1951 US–Denmark defence treaty for Greenland. According to DW, it also covers Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, keeps Greenland under Danish control and restates Greenlanders' right to self-determination. Pele Broberg, leader of the pro-independence Naleraq party, said Greenland had gained no economic benefit from it. It takes effect only after the Danish parliament ratifies it; a vote is scheduled in Copenhagen on Thursday 19 November.
story.why: the deal is the result of Trump's threats in January to take control of Greenland, and it gives the US a bigger military footprint in the Arctic without a change of sovereignty.

story.headline: Spanish transport minister quits after crash
story.summary: Spanish transport minister Óscar Puente resigned on 3 November after the 28 October high-speed train collision that killed 69 people.
story.display_body: Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday 3 November, six days after a high-speed train collision on the Madrid–Seville line killed at least 69 people on Wednesday 28 October. He told parliament that a transport minister "cannot continue in office with two accidents of this severity in less than a year", referring also to the January derailment at Adamuz in Andalusia that killed 46. He also withdrew from the candidate lists for the early general election of Sunday 29 November. Early findings are that, after a computer failure stopped several trains, the control centre in Madrid wrongly told one train to continue, and it hit a stationary train. The government announced a €30 million aid package for victims and their families.

story.headline: Federal Court rules out most website blocks
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court ruled that prosecutors lack a legal basis to order ISPs to block websites outside specific laws, upholding Init7's appeal against Vaud.
story.display_body: Prosecutors cannot order internet providers to block websites except where a specific law allows it, the Federal Supreme Court said on Wednesday 4 November, upholding an appeal by the provider Init7 against the Vaud public prosecutor. In July 2025 the Vaud prosecutor ordered several providers to block access to the web addresses of an alleged online investment fraud (a DNS block, which stops the domain name from resolving). SRF reports that the fraud cost investors more than CHF 1.7 million. The prosecutor relied on the general rules on seizure in the Criminal Procedure Code. The court, in a judgment dated Monday 12 October (7B_52/2026), ruled that these rules are not a sufficient legal basis. Parliament has allowed blocking only in specific cases: unlicensed online gambling, illegal pornography and, temporarily, domains in unfair-competition proceedings. The court said blocking can be an effective tool against online fraud, but that deciding when to allow it, who orders it and on what conditions is for the federal legislator.
story.why: Swiss prosecutors lose a tool they had been using against online scams, and whether to give it back is now a question for parliament.

story.headline: Pension minimum interest rate rises to 2%
story.summary: The Federal Council raised the BVG/LPP minimum interest rate from 1.25% to 2% from January 2027.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 4 November raised the minimum interest rate on mandatory occupational-pension (BVG/LPP) savings from 1.25% to 2% from January 2027, above the 1.75% its advisory commission recommended on 4 September. The government says 2% matches the commission's own formula as of the end of September. It points to pension funds' average returns of 6.1% in 2025 and 5.4% to the end of August 2026, and an average funding ratio of 122.5% for funds without a state guarantee. In its words, the increase "compensates the relatively high inflation observed since 2022". The social partners had argued for rates from 1.25% to 3%. The minimum applies only to the mandatory part of retirement savings; funds set their own rate on savings above that level.
story.why: most employees in Switzerland will see a higher guaranteed return on their pension savings next year, and the rate is now above October's 1.5% inflation.

story.headline: Bern proposes looser CO2 target for vans
story.summary: The Federal Council opened a consultation on loosening 2030 CO2 targets for vans and tightening them for heavy lorries, in line with the EU.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 4 November proposed a weaker CO2 target for new vans from 2030 and a stricter one for heavy lorries, following the EU, and opened a consultation that runs until Thursday 18 February 2027. For light commercial vehicles registered from 2030, the target would be 108.7 g CO2/km instead of the 90.6 g/km in current law. For heavy lorries, the required cut in emissions from 2030 would rise from 30% to 45%. Importers of cars and vans would also be allowed to average their emissions over 2030–2032 instead of meeting the target every year. The government also wants to adopt the EU's standard energy label for vehicles.

story.headline: Switzerland taps kerosene reserves again
story.summary: The federal supply delegate authorised a second release of up to 50,000 m3 of kerosene from compulsory reserves due to refinery restrictions in France and Germany.
story.display_body: On Tuesday 3 November, the federal delegate for economic supply authorised up to 50,000 m³ of kerosene to be released from compulsory reserves until Sunday 29 November, the second release in a few weeks. This shortage is due to restrictions at refineries in southern France and Germany. Together with October's 30,000 m³, 17.4% of the kerosene reserve has now been made available; the delegate can authorise up to 20% before the economics department has to issue an ordinance. The release is mainly for Geneva and Zurich airports. Oil supply has been tight for months because the Rhine is hard to navigate, and reserves have been used four times since September.

story.headline: Carbon pentaheptite ribbon conducts like a metal
story.summary: Graphene is built from hexagons.
story.display_body: Graphene is built from hexagons. Theorists have long predicted that a flat carbon sheet made of five- and seven-membered rings, called a "pentaheptite", would be a metal rather than a semiconductor, but nobody had made a clean strip of one. The Hefei team grew the ribbons on a metal surface in steps. They first made chains of eight-membered rings, turned those into chains of fused pentagon pairs (polypentalene), then zipped neighbouring chains together sideways. This gives a ribbon a few atoms wide with a heptagon spine. Two variants came out. In one (CPHN 1) the edge chains point the same way, and it is an intrinsic metal with near-ballistic conductance approaching one conductance quantum. That is the ideal limit for a single conducting channel, the same benchmark metallic carbon nanotubes reach. The other variant is a narrow-gap semiconductor. The authors say the synthesis still needs work before the ribbons can go into devices.
story.why: all-carbon chips need both semiconductors and wires made of the same chemistry, and this is a flat, atomically precise carbon wire that can be built on a surface alongside graphene-nanoribbon transistors.

story.headline: Silicone waste unzipped back to monomer
story.summary: Silicones are prized because they are thermally and chemically inert, and that is exactly why they are so hard to recycle.
story.display_body: Silicones are prized because they are thermally and chemically inert, and that is exactly why they are so hard to recycle. Today they are landfilled, burned, ground up, or at best broken down into cyclic siloxanes. Martin Oestreich's group at TU Berlin breaks the Si–O–Si backbone outright and gets back dichlorosilane, the industrial monomer silicones are made from. The reagent is phosgene or its safer liquid substitutes, triggered by a silylium ion (a highly reactive silicon cation). Calculations with Bonn's Mulliken Center show that phosgene is not just a chloride donor. The silylium ion activates it into a chlorocarbonyl cation, and that cation does the cutting. The process works under mild conditions on commercial silicone oils and elastomers as well as model siloxanes. It is a laboratory demonstration: the paper reports no industrial-scale throughput or energy balance, and phosgene handling is a real constraint.
story.why: this is a route to true closed-loop recycling for one of the few large-volume polymer families with no such option, developed in Germany, which is home to much of Europe's silicone industry.

story.headline: Graphene electrons filmed tunnelling between bands
story.summary: When a strong light wave pushes an electron through a crystal's energy bands, the electron can jump to a higher band at points where two bands nearly touch.
story.display_body: When a strong light wave pushes an electron through a crystal's energy bands, the electron can jump to a higher band at points where two bands nearly touch. This jump is Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling, a textbook quantum process: a system forced quickly through an "avoided crossing" may hop to the other level instead of following its own. It has been theorized for decades in strong-field solids but never seen directly across the whole crystal. The German team combined terahertz-driven graphene with photoelectron momentum microscopy, which images electrons by direction and energy, at attosecond timing precision. The result is a frame-by-frame "video" of where the electrons sit across the entire first Brillouin zone, the full map of electron momentum states, within one oscillation of the driving field. The tunnelling shows up as a coherent shift and distortion of the electron cloud at the zone edge, repeating every half-cycle. The data also separate the scattering processes that destroy the coherent motion.
story.why: "lightwave electronics", which switches currents with light fields at petahertz speeds, depends on exactly this tunnelling, and now it can be watched instead of inferred. Jülich's participation puts a German national lab at the centre of the instrumentation.

story.headline: Single molecule works as quantum-network node
story.summary: A quantum network needs nodes that store a qubit in a spin, a long-lived magnetic orientation, and can hand it to a photon on request.
story.display_body: A quantum network needs nodes that store a qubit in a spin, a long-lived magnetic orientation, and can hand it to a photon on request. Today's leading nodes are defects in diamond and similar crystals. Those defects cannot be designed atom by atom, and no two are quite alike. This team used a carbene, a molecule with two unpaired electrons whose ground state is a spin triplet, embedded in a matching host crystal. At 4.5 K a single such molecule gave sharp optical lines, the zero-phonon lines that mark clean, photon-ready transitions. Its colour stayed stable for more than an hour. It showed spin-selective transitions and could be read out through optically detected magnetic resonance. Pulse sequences kept its spin coherent for milliseconds, and spin flips took tens of milliseconds. Diamond defects still outperform it, so this is a proof that the platform works, not a better qubit yet.
story.why: if molecules can match defects, quantum nodes could be made by chemists in identical batches. The work comes from Ulm and NVision, an Ulm spin-out.

story.headline: Hard X-ray pulses timed to 170 attoseconds
story.summary: X-ray free-electron lasers such as SLAC's LCLS can now make hard X-ray pulses short enough to follow electrons moving inside molecules.
story.display_body: X-ray free-electron lasers such as SLAC's LCLS can now make hard X-ray pulses short enough to follow electrons moving inside molecules. One attosecond is 10⁻¹⁸ s, and an electron orbit takes about 100 of them. So far nobody could measure how long those pulses actually were. The team split each pulse into two copies with a broadband delay line and scanned the delay between them. Field correlation gave the first time-domain measurement of the pulses' coherence time and showed that the two copies were synchronized to attoseconds. They then used non-sequential two-photon absorption, in which an atom absorbs two X-ray photons only when both arrive together, as a stopwatch. This intensity autocorrelation gives an average pulse duration of 170 attoseconds.
story.why: without a trustworthy ruler, attosecond X-ray experiments could not be compared or repeated. This turns X-ray-pump/X-ray-probe studies of electron motion into a calibrated method, which matters for facilities including PSI's SwissFEL in Villigen.

story.headline: Fermilab's SBND finds no argon model fits
story.summary: The Short-Baseline Near Detector is a liquid-argon detector at Fermilab that saw its first neutrinos in 2024.
story.display_body: The Short-Baseline Near Detector is a liquid-argon detector at Fermilab that saw its first neutrinos in 2024. Its first physics paper measures how muon neutrinos interact with argon when the visible products are a muon, exactly one proton and no pions. Out of 8.8×10¹⁹ protons on target (a subset of Run 1), it selected 12,804 such events at 91% purity. The analysis uses "transverse kinematic imbalance": in a free collision, momentum sideways to the beam should balance. Any leftover imbalance measures what the nucleus did: the motion of the struck proton and its re-scattering on the way out. None of the event generators compared reproduces all three measured variables, and the transverse missing momentum shows the biggest discrepancies. The paper has been submitted to Physical Review Letters but is not yet peer reviewed. Fermilab's release describes it as groundwork for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), whose beam is due by 2031.
story.why: DUNE's search for matter–antimatter asymmetry in neutrinos rests on modelling exactly these argon interactions, and SBND's statistics can now rule models out instead of merely bracketing them. CERN's neutrino platform built prototypes for DUNE, so the problem matters to European physicists too.

story.headline: Moon's retreat may have shoved early crust
story.summary: After the Moon-forming impact, Earth spun fast enough to bulge strongly at the equator.
story.display_body: After the Moon-forming impact, Earth spun fast enough to bulge strongly at the equator. As tides pushed the Moon outward over the first tens of millions of years, Earth's spin slowed and the planet relaxed toward a sphere. Simon Lock combined planetary-structure and tidal-evolution calculations to ask what that change of shape did to the earliest crust. He finds that the first crust would have been thicker or thinner depending on latitude. As Earth rounded out, the crust would have stretched near the poles and been compressed near the equator, in high-angular-momentum scenarios at rates comparable to the Himalayas forming today. Depending on how stiff that crust was, the motion could have buried wet, weathered surface rock, driven volcanism and released gas from the interior. This is a modelling study with one author. No rock record has yet tested it, and few fragments of Earth's first crust survive.
story.why: it puts a new, ignored driver of early plate-like tectonics into the debate over how and when continental crust first formed, and it makes specific predictions that ancient zircons could check.

He finds that the first crust would have been thicker or thinner depending on latitude. As Earth rounded out, the crust would have stretched near the poles and been compressed near the equator, in high-angular-momentum scenarios at rates comparable to the Himalayas forming today. Depending on how stiff that crust was, the motion could have buried wet, weathered surface rock, driven volcanism and released gas from the interior. This is a modelling study with one author. No rock record has yet tested it, and few fragments of Earth's first crust survive.
fields.why: it puts a new, ignored driver of early plate-like tectonics into the debate over how and when continental crust first formed, and it makes specific predictions that ancient zircons could check.

story.headline: Eukaryotes' closest archaeal kin grown at last
story.summary: All complex life, from yeast to people, is thought to have arisen from an archaeon (a single-celled microbe without a nucleus) in the Asgard group, now formally called Promethearchaeota, that merged with the bacterium which became the mitochondrion.
story.display_body: All complex life, from yeast to people, is thought to have arisen from an archaeon (a single-celled microbe without a nucleus) in the Asgard group, now formally called Promethearchaeota, that merged with the bacterium which became the mitochondrion. Genomes put a subgroup called Heimdallarchaeia closest to eukaryotes. Some researchers had predicted those microbes would already have eukaryote-like internal membranes and breathe oxygen. JAMSTEC's Hiroyuki Imachi and Masaru Nobu isolated the first two cultured Heimdallarchaeia strains, HC1 and SC1, grown in co-culture with methane-producing partners. The team did the same for the more distant Asgard strain MK-D1 in 2020. Neither strain has any persistent internal membrane. Both are anaerobic, digest peptides, depend on partner microbes, and extend long protrusions and vesicles to cling to their neighbours. HC1 carries an oxygen-handling enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase. It still cannot grow with oxygen present unless oxygen-consuming bacteria are nearby, which suggests the enzyme detoxifies oxygen rather than powering respiration. Comparative genomics suggests the same holds for other Heimdallarchaeia.
story.why: the best available stand-in for our archaeal ancestor is simple inside and sociable outside. That supports a scenario in which the partnership with the mitochondrial ancestor began in low-oxygen conditions and internal complexity came later, and it gives labs a living model to test eukaryogenesis experimentally.

story.headline: Heart mitochondria import lactate directly
story.summary: Textbook metabolism says sugar is broken down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm.
story.display_body: Textbook metabolism says sugar is broken down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm. Pyruvate then enters mitochondria through one door, the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC), to be burned. The Utah-led team found that mouse hearts lacking MPC still burn glucose carbon. The workaround is MCT1, a lactate transporter normally found on the outer cell membrane. In mouse and human heart cells it also sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Together with the enzyme LDHB inside the mitochondrion, it converts imported lactate to pyruvate and NADH, feeding the electron transport chain directly. Mice lacking MCT1 lost metabolic flexibility. They developed heart failure faster and died more often after hormonal overdrive (neurohormonal hyperactivation) or after blood flow was cut and restored (ischaemia–reperfusion, a model of heart attack). The evidence is from mouse genetics, with human cardiomyocytes used only to show that the protein is there.
story.why: it identifies a second carbohydrate-fuel pathway that the stressed heart depends on, and with it a candidate target or liability for heart-failure drugs that act on metabolism.

story.headline: Connectome simulation finds fly walking circuit
story.summary: Walking depends on central pattern generators (CPGs), circuits that produce a rhythm without needing rhythmic input.
story.display_body: Walking depends on central pattern generators (CPGs), circuits that produce a rhythm without needing rhythmic input. No one had pinned down the actual wiring of a walking CPG in any animal. The Seattle team ran dynamic simulations on full wiring diagrams (connectomes) of the fruit fly's nerve cord, the insect counterpart of the spinal cord. An in-silico screen of descending command neurons picked out DNg100, a known "walk" command neuron, as the strongest rhythm driver. Pruning the simulated network left a minimal oscillator of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons. That circuit was necessary and sufficient for rhythm in all six legs, across four independent connectome datasets. The simulations also predicted that a second command neuron, DNb08, drives leg rhythms, and optogenetic stimulation of live flies confirmed it. The paper calls the circuit a "putative" CPG: its necessity in living flies has not yet been fully tested.
story.why: it is one of the first cases where a connectome predicted a behavioural circuit that was then confirmed in the animal, turning wiring maps from atlases into hypothesis generators.

story.headline: Ancient meteorite samples early Martian crust
story.summary: Most of the roughly 435 known Martian meteorites are geologically young volcanic rocks, while most of Mars' surface is ancient.
story.display_body: Most of the roughly 435 known Martian meteorites are geologically young volcanic rocks, while most of Mars' surface is ancient. Teghaza 001 is an 800-gram rose-coloured stone found in 2022 on a salt plain in Mali. It is a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago, which makes it one of the three oldest Martian meteorites known. Its composition, minerals and texture differ from every other Martian meteorite. The team concludes it is ancient crust that crystallized from a chemically distinct mantle source with primordial composition. Altered minerals and oxygen-isotope ratios show it reacted with water enriched in oxygen-18 before an impact blasted it into space. According to JPL, its mineralogy matches what the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter sees in the cratered southern highlands. Its exact launch site cannot be known.
story.why: until samples are returned from Mars, this is the best physical record of Mars' early crust and of how water acted on it while the planet was losing its atmosphere.

story.headline: New glare model reveals planet in JWST data
story.summary: To photograph a planet next to its star, astronomers block the star with a coronagraph, then subtract the leftover glare using a reference image.
story.display_body: To photograph a planet next to its star, astronomers block the star with a coronagraph, then subtract the leftover glare using a reference image. Even tiny telescope drifts between the reference and science exposures leave residue that hides faint planets. The team instead built a flexible physical model of the starlight, including the instrument's instabilities, and fitted millions of parameters with automatic differentiation, the gradient machinery behind modern optimization. On real JWST NIRCam coronagraph data it was 2–15 times more sensitive than standard methods. It delivered the first detection of the young giant planet 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm, a wavelength band that tracks carbon-bearing molecules in the planet's atmosphere. The authors present it as a demonstration on existing data, not a new survey.
story.why: it relaxes the extreme stability requirements of future planet imagers such as Roman and the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which is a key cost and risk driver in the hunt for Earth-like exoplanets.

story.headline: Twin feeding black holes in early merger
story.summary: When galaxies merge, their central supermassive black holes eventually spiral together.
story.display_body: When galaxies merge, their central supermassive black holes eventually spiral together. Before that, they should pass through a "dual AGN" phase, in which both actively feed and shine only a few thousand light-years apart. Such close pairs are rare in surveys of the early Universe. LID-1166, at redshift 4.5, is one: two nuclei separated by about 1.5 kiloparsecs (~5,000 light-years). JWST's NIRSpec spatially resolved spectroscopy shows two distinct narrow-line emission sources, separated by about 164 km/s in velocity. Each also shows broad hydrogen-alpha emission, the mark of gas whirling close to an accreting black hole. ALMA independently resolved separate cold-gas clouds on each nucleus, confirming that this is a gas-rich merger. Both black holes are accreting above the Eddington rate, the nominal limit for steady feeding. Yet they already sit on the black-hole-to-host-mass relation of today's giant elliptical galaxies, which suggests that obscured, merger-driven growth sets that relation early. One object cannot establish a population. The "missing population" the authors propose is an inference.
story.why: such pairs are the progenitors of the gravitational-wave background that pulsar timing arrays now detect and that ESA's LISA mission is designed to hear directly.
